title: The TCP SYN Scan: How Professionals Map Open Ports
content:
You know what a port is. You know why it exists. The question now is: how do you find out which ports on a remote host are open — without any credentials or prior access?

The answer is the TCP SYN scan. It is Nmap's default scanning method and the professional standard for port discovery on every penetration test.

**Why the TCP handshake is the key**

Recall from Mission 1: when two computers want to establish a TCP connection, they go through three steps:

1. Your machine sends a **SYN** packet: 'I want to connect.'
2. If a service is listening on that port, the target responds: **SYN/ACK** — 'Yes, let's connect.'
3. Your machine sends **ACK**: 'Great, we are connected.'

Step 3 completes the connection. Both sides enter a fully established TCP session.

Here is the key insight: **you do not need step 3 to learn whether a port is open.**

The SYN/ACK in step 2 already tells you everything. A SYN/ACK means a service is listening and the port is open. An RST instead of SYN/ACK means the host is alive but the port is closed. You can learn both facts without completing the handshake.

**How the SYN scan works**

The SYN scan sends a SYN packet to each target port and classifies the port based on the response:

- **SYN/ACK received → port is OPEN.** A service is listening. It accepted the incoming connection request.
- **RST received → port is CLOSED.** The host is alive but nothing is listening on this port. The host itself rejected the probe.
- **No response → port is FILTERED.** A firewall intercepted the SYN before it reached the host. The state of the port is unknown.

When a port responds with SYN/ACK (open), Nmap immediately sends RST to tear down the half-open connection. The handshake is never completed. Nmap learned what it needed and withdrew without establishing a full session.

**Why this matters: what the half-open technique gives you**

Many application-layer systems — web server logs, SSH daemon logs, database audit logs — only record fully-established connections. A connection that goes SYN → SYN/ACK → RST (instead of SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK) may not appear in those logs at all.

This does not make the SYN scan invisible — network devices and dedicated IDS systems can still detect it. But it reduces the footprint compared to a full connect scan, which completes the handshake and is much more likely to leave records.

**The command**

```
# Standard professional port scan
nmap -sS -T4 -oA port-scan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10
```

Flag breakdown:
- **-sS** — TCP SYN scan (the default; included here explicitly for learning clarity)
- **-T4** — Timing: fast. Reliable for standard internet connections without causing packet loss
- **-oA port-scan-45.77.180.10** — Save all three output formats simultaneously, named for the target

Additional useful variations:

```
# Scan specific ports only
nmap -sS -p 22,80,443,8080,8443,3306 45.77.180.10

# Full range — all 65,535 ports (essential for thorough assessments)
nmap -sS -p- -T4 -oA fullscan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10

# Without root: TCP connect scan (equivalent results, slower and more visible)
nmap -sT -T4 -oA port-scan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10
```

**Why the SYN scan is the professional default**

Four reasons professionals reach for -sS on every engagement:

1. **Speed.** No session maintenance. Probes go out, responses come back, state is recorded. Faster than completing handshakes.
2. **Reduced footprint.** Half-open connections may not appear in application-layer logs.
3. **Reliable results.** All three port states are distinguishable — SYN/ACK for open, RST for closed, silence for filtered.
4. **Universal understanding.** When a professional writes 'TCP SYN scan' in a report, every reader knows exactly what technique was used, what the results mean, and what the scan's limitations are.

callouts.title: Root / Administrator Required
callouts.text: The SYN scan sends raw packets, which requires root on Linux/macOS or Administrator on Windows. Without elevated privileges, Nmap automatically falls back to the TCP connect scan (-sT), which completes the full three-way handshake. On Kali Linux — the standard penetration testing platform — root access is typically assumed. If you see 'Permission denied' when running -sS, check that you are running with sudo or as root.

callouts.title: Always Save Output — The Professional Standard
callouts.text:
Every scan you run should be saved to a file before you start interpreting results. The -oA flag saves three formats simultaneously:

• .nmap — human-readable plain text
• .xml — machine-readable, imports into reporting tools
• .gnmap — grepable, for filtering with command-line tools

Name the file with the target IP and scan type: -oA port-scan-45.77.180.10

This turns your output folder into self-documenting evidence — you can reconstruct exactly what was run, against which target, at what time, without relying on memory.

keyTerms.definition: Nmap's default port scanning method. Sends a TCP SYN packet to each target port and classifies the port based on the response: SYN/ACK = open, RST = closed, no response = filtered. Never completes the three-way handshake. Requires root or administrator privileges to send raw packets.

A TCP connection that was initiated (SYN sent and SYN/ACK received) but never completed (no ACK was sent). The SYN scan works by creating and immediately abandoning half-open connections — which is what makes it faster and potentially less visible than a full connect scan.

An alternative port scanning method that completes the full three-way handshake. Does not require root privileges because it uses the OS's standard network socket calls. Slower and more visible than the SYN scan. Used when root access is unavailable.

# Standard SYN scan — professional default
nmap -sS -T4 -oA port-scan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10

# Scan specific known ports
nmap -sS -p 22,80,443,3306,8080,8443 45.77.180.10

# Full-range scan — all 65,535 ports (run on every high-priority target)
nmap -sS -p- -T4 -oA fullscan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10

# Without root: TCP connect scan (equivalent results, slower)
nmap -sT -T4 -oA port-scan-45.77.180.10 45.77.180.10
